Writ Petition No. 189 of 1976.
In the matter of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
lawyer:
S. R. Pail with S.C Das & Zakir Ahmed  -----For the Petitioner. 
Syed J. R. Mudadsir Hossain -----For Respondents No. 1 & 2.
parties:
Srimongal Pourashava ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms & others ----- Respondents.

3. In this connection reference may be made to the provisions of Hats and Bazars (Establishment) and Acquisition Ordinance 1959 (Ordinance No XIX of 1959). Sub-section (1) of section 2 of the said Ordinance provides that no person shall establish any hats and bazars except without a license for that purpose from the Collector in such form as may be prescribed by rules. Sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Ordinance provides that any hats and bazars established in contravention of the aforesaid provisions shall be forfeited to the Government. Hats and Bazars (Establishment) and Acquisition (Amendment) Act of 1966 (Act XII/67) had amended the provisions of section 2 of the aforesaid Ordinance No. XIX of 1959 where under at present no person shall establish any hats or bazars excepting the Government or any local authority with the approval of the Government The local authority means local-councils as defined in sub clause (24) of clause 1 of Article 3 of the Basic Democracy Ordinance of 1959 and subsequently it included a Municipal Committee under the Municipal Administration Ordinance 1960 followed by the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. Subsequently Bangladesh Government Hats and Bazars (Management) Order of 1972 (P.O. 73/72) was introduced providing for the management of all Government hats and bazars. P.O. No. 73 of 1972 stood repealed by Bangladesh Government Hats and bazars (Management Repeal) Ordinance 1975 (Ordinance No. 59 of 1975). Considering the aforesaid provisions of law it now appears that there is no special provisions for management of Government hats and Bazars but the Government has an absolute right to establish any hat and bazar. A local authority including a Municipality or Pourashava can also establish a hat and bazar with the prior approval of the Government. All the references made to the various provisions of law made herein-before are prospective in nature providing for powers of the Government and any local authority including a Pourashava to establish and to maintain any hat or bazar or a market as the case may be after the promulgation of the laws referred to hereinbefore. The aforesaid statutes are completely silent with regard to the powers of the Government to take over such hats and bazars and markets in possession of a local authority like a Pourashava. It appears that apart front the general provisions of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there is no other special statutory provisions authorising the Government to acquire and to take over any hat and bazar and market already remaining under the ownership and possession of a local authority and a Pourashava. 

 4. Under sub-section (1) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, on acquisition of the interests of rent-receiver in any area under Chapter V of the Act no rent receiver, cultivating raiyat, cultivating under raiyat or non-agricultural tenant shall be entitled to retain any khash land in such area except as provided in sub-section (2) thereof. By virtue of the provisions of section (2) (a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act any land or building in a hat or bazar have been excluded from the retainable khash land contemplated under sub-section (2) thereof. Now the question is whether any,land or building in a hat or bazar which inevitably includes a market as such can be retained by a local authority like a Pourashava. In the category of persons who are entitled to retain possession of any khash land under sub-section (1) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act a Municipality or Pourashava does not come within the definition of a rent-receiver or a cultivating raiyat or under raiyot as such. As to the non-agricultural tenant, it appears from the definition thereof from sub-section (17) of section 2 with reference to State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also with reference to the definition of tenant as provided in sub-section (27) of section 2 the said Act, it appears that the language used thereunder is "a tenant" meaning "a person". There is no statutory provision whereby a local authority like a Municipality or a Pourashava has been specifically omitted from being a person like a tenant under the Government Thee scheme of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which extends to the whole of Bangladesh, contemplates only 4 classes of persons who can own lands under the Government as aforesaid and there is no other class as such. In such circumstances a Pourashava for the purpose of owning and holding any land is a tenant under the Government. From the paltan of the Srimongal Pourashava relating to the markets in question it also appears that the Government has been shown. as the landlord and the Srimongal Municipality as aperson in possession thereof. Considering the aforesaid circumstances it must be held that the Government can acquire and take over any hat or bazar including a market since the lands thereunder are non-retainable by any tenant. But in the absence of any specific proceeding under Chapter V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, non-retainable hat or bazar or market of a Municipality or Pourashava is not liable to be acquired by the Government. Thus acquisition of any Municipal market by the Government can only proceed according to the provisions of Chapter V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act culminating in the final publication of the compensation Assessment roll under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Only after such publication the Government by a special order takes possession of any market belonging to any Pourashava. In this connection it may be mentioned that subject to the ultimate right of the Government to acquire and take over any Municipal market, a Municipality or a Pourashava can establish and run any market as provided under sections 84 and 85 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. 

 5. Considering the aforesaid provisions of law the position is that a Pourashava can establish and maintain a new market under section 84 and 85 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977, with the permission of the Government as contemplated under Ordinance No. XIX of 1959 as amended by Act No. XII of 1967 With regard to such markets which existed before coming into force of the provisions of Ordinance No XIX of 1959 as amended by Act XII of 1967, the Government is not prevented from acquiring and taking over any such old markets under the provisions of sub-section 2 (a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But in any case to enable the Government to acquire and to take over any such Municipal market there must be an order to that effect after the final publication of the compensation assessment roll in the Official Gazette under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Be that as it may, admittedly in the present case there is nothing on record to show that there has been any final publication of the compensation assessment roll in the Official Gazette with regard to the areas in question under the Srimongal Pourashava and further admit only there is no order specifically acquiring the markets in question of the Srimongal Municipality as such. In that view of the matter it must be held that the decision of the Government to take over the markets in question of the Srimongal Municipality was done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. As such the decision of the Government as communicated to the petitioner by Annexures B and 1 to the petition am set aside. This rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs.
